findings.title: Divergent affective reactions to reduced structure/openness within I01
findings.description: Within the same interview, students give directly conflicting evaluations of the open-ended, less-defined nature of the lab: one student frames the freedom to discuss and derive results as enjoyable, while another explicitly says the experience was 'not as fun' and less defined than expected.

findings.title: Cross-interview preference for hands-on, intuitive engagement over rigid procedure
findings.description: Students in both interviews independently express a preference for direct, hands-on, exploratory engagement with equipment/results over predetermined or heavily procedural work, describing it as more constructive, freeing, or intuitive.

findings.title: Enjoyment of reduced data-collection burden reveals an implicit contrast with other labs' demands
findings.description: Statements praising this lab for not requiring extensive data collection only make sense as a comparative judgment against other labs in the course, which are implied to be stressful due to heavy data-taking; this contrast is not visible from the code counts alone, only by reading the quote content together with its context of comparison to 'first years' and 'other labs'.

findings.title: Overlap between enjoyment (2.a/3.b) and conceptual engagement (2.c/3.a) suggests hands-on play is the mechanism linking affect and learning
findings.description: The same quotes about 'playing' with the setup and turning knobs intuitively are coded both as preference/enjoyment and as experimentalist identity or learning gain, suggesting that in students' accounts, enjoyment and conceptual understanding are not separate outcomes but are produced through the same hands-on exploratory activity. This pattern is visible only by cross-referencing quotes across codes, not from counts alone.

findings.title: Tension between valuing lack of theoretical scaffolding as freeing versus needing background knowledge to function
findings.description: In I01, one student frames the open-ended lack of predetermined results as a positive ('nice to talk more freely'), while other students in the same interview state they would have had 'no idea' what they were doing without prior optics background and found the pre-lab explanation too fast to fully grasp, indicating the same lack of structure was experienced as a barrier by others.

findings.title: Lab as a vehicle for specialization/career orientation, not just conceptual learning
findings.description: Some quotes describe the lab's value not in terms of immediate conceptual understanding or enjoyment but in terms of exposure to a possible future specialization or field relevance (e.g., informatics, laser physics, quantum specialization), a forward-looking career-orientation theme that is only partially captured by the existing 'usefulness' code and recurs distinctly from enjoyment/learning codes.

findings.title: Direct conflict over perceived relevance of lab topic to students' field of study
findings.description: In I01, a student explicitly states the quantum-related lab content is 'not really our area' for most of the group (astrophysics students), directly contrasting with statements in I02 where students find the same type of content engaging and relevant to potential future specialization, highlighting a relevance/mismatch issue that varies by group composition.
